data.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
data.summary: State-changing requests were authorised by the session cookie alone, with no unpredictable value tying the request to the application's own interface. A page under an attacker's control could therefore cause a logged-in user's browser to perform actions on their behalf.
data.description:
The browser attaches cookies for a site to any request made to it, regardless of which page caused the request. An application that treats the presence of a session cookie as proof of intent will act on requests that the user never meant to make.

The user's involvement is limited to visiting a page while logged in. The attacker sees neither the response nor the session, so CSRF is an integrity issue: changing an email address or password, transferring funds, granting a role, or altering configuration.

`SameSite=Lax`, now the default in major browsers, removes much of the classic exposure but is not a complete control: it does not apply to top-level `GET` navigations, and applications that perform state changes on `GET` remain reachable.
data.recommendation:
* Issue an unpredictable anti-CSRF token per session, require it on every state-changing request, and verify it server-side.
* Set `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` on session cookies as defence in depth.
* Never perform state changes on `GET`.
* For APIs consumed by browsers, verify `Origin` against an allow-list.
* Require re-authentication for high-value changes such as password and email updates.
data.short_recommendation: Require anti-CSRF tokens and set SameSite on session cookies.
